vignette:
Daniel Varga, a 32-year-old European American combat pilot, came to treatment after months of living as though danger might break into any ordinary hour. The assault had happened after a rare night off, when he had gone out for drinks with a colleague he trusted and accepted a ride home from someone who seemed harmless enough. What Daniel remembered most was the betrayal of that trust: the ease with which the situation had shifted from familiar to unsafe, and how powerless he had felt once he realized he had been misled. Since then, he had come to believe that what happened said something damning about him. He described himself as a lousy coper, someone whose reactions had been pathetic compared with what he believed a man in his position should be able to withstand, and he spoke with a bitter sense that he had lost his faith in people, in life, and in any higher power that might have been watching. Those beliefs did not sit in the background for him; they colored the whole world. Because he felt betrayed and morally exposed, he became watchful for any hint that someone might be suspicious, and even a stranger pausing too long near his building or a neighbor lingering in the hallway could set off an immediate, uneasy alarm.

In the weeks after the assault, Daniel found himself listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering his apartment. He kept checking the lock twice, then three times, then going back again if he heard footsteps in the corridor or a lift door open downstairs. Ordinary noises would make him jump in a way that embarrassed him: a dropped pan in the kitchen, the abrupt slam of a car door outside, a late-night text notification. At home, where he had once felt most competent and in control, he now felt on guard, his body never fully settling. The more keyed up he became, the more he searched for reasons to stay alert. That constant scanning fed his earlier belief that people could not be trusted, and it made every ambiguous moment feel charged. He was especially vulnerable after waking from a nightmare, when he would sit upright in bed, heart racing, already half-convinced that whatever had happened in sleep might still be waiting somewhere in the room. On those mornings, he found himself watching faces on the street and in the grocery store with unusual suspicion, certain that a person who seemed oddly polite, too interested, or simply hard to read might be dangerous.

As the months passed, those beliefs and that alertness tightened around one another. Daniel’s conviction that he had been betrayed by someone he trusted made him more alert to suspicious behavior, and the more he stayed on guard, the more his body behaved as if danger were imminent: a startle at ordinary sounds, a readiness to flinch, an inability to relax even in his own apartment. He began to interpret his own ongoing vigilance as further proof that he was failing to cope, as though his nervous system’s refusal to stand down exposed weakness in him. That appraisal, in turn, deepened his sense that he could not trust anyone, which made social situations feel threatening and unpredictable. He started declining invitations from fellow pilots after work and avoiding the easy camaraderie that had once helped him decompress. Because unpredictability had become especially difficult, he planned his days with rigid precision, choosing the same routes, the same coffee shop, the same parking spot, and feeling increasingly unsettled whenever a schedule changed without warning. Even in the cockpit, where he was outwardly disciplined, he found himself more sensitive to unexpected radio static or an abrupt change in tone, his attention snapping toward anything that might signal an unseen threat. The more he noticed his own reactions, the more convinced he became that they were evidence of failure, and that sense of failure sharpened his suspicion that people were not what they seemed.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by the strain of living with his home as a place of constant watchfulness. He had started sleeping poorly because he dreaded the moment of waking from a nightmare and the instant of disorientation that followed, and he was afraid that if he kept going like this, his career and the few remaining relationships he valued would narrow even further. What finally brought him in was a recent night when he startled hard at a harmless noise in his apartment, then spent the next hour listening at the door, ashamed of how unsafe he felt in a place he was supposed to control. He said he wanted to stop feeling as though every strange face and every unexpected sound might mean another betrayal was about to begin, but what frightened him most was that part of him had already stopped believing he could ever fully trust people again.
